units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Yes; that is quite, quite true. I had not thought of that.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Enter SIR JOHN and MR. KELVIL.
Well, Mr. Kelvil, have you got through your work?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I have finished my writing for the day, Lady Hunstanton. It has been an arduous task. The demands on the time of a public man are very heavy nowadays, very heavy indeed. And I don’t think they meet with adequate recognition.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: John, have you got your overshoes on?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Yes, my love.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: I think you had better come over here, John. It is more sheltered.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: I am quite comfortable, Caroline.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: I think not, John. You had better sit beside me.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: SIR JOHN rises and goes across .
And what have you been writing about this morning, Mr. Kelvil?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: On the usual subject, Lady Stutfield. On Purity.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: That must be such a very, very interesting thing to write about.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: It is the one subject of really national importance, nowadays, Lady Stutfield. I purpose addressing my constituents on the question before Parliament meets. I find that the poorer classes of this country display a marked desire for a higher ethical standard.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: How quite, quite nice of them.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Are you in favour of women taking part in politics, Mr. Kettle?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Kelvil, my love, Kelvil.
units.name: SIR JOHN

units.text: The growing influence of women is the one reassuring thing in our political life, Lady Caroline. Women are always on the side of morality, public and private.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: It is so very, very gratifying to hear you say that.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Ah, yes!—the moral qualities in women—that is the important thing. I am afraid, Caroline, that dear Lord Illingworth doesn’t value the moral qualities in women as much as he should.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Enter LORD ILLINGWORTH.
The world says that Lord Illingworth is very, very wicked.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: But what world says that, Lady Stutfield? It must be the next world. This world and I are on excellent terms.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Sits down beside MRS. ALLONBY.
Every one I know says you are very, very wicked.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: It is perfectly monstrous the way people go about, nowadays, saying things against one behind one’s back that are absolutely and entirely true.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Dear Lord Illingworth is quite hopeless, Lady Stutfield. I have given up trying to reform him. It would take a Public Company with a Board of Directors and a paid Secretary to do that. But you have the secretary already, Lord Illingworth, haven’t you? Gerald Arbuthnot has told us of his good fortune; it is really most kind of you.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Oh, don’t say that, Lady Hunstanton. Kind is a dreadful word. I took a great fancy to young Arbuthnot the moment I met him, and he’ll be of considerable use to me in something I am foolish enough to think of doing.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: He is an admirable young man. And his mother is one of my dearest friends. He has just gone for a walk with our pretty American. She is very pretty, is she not?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Far too pretty. These American girls carry off all the good matches. Why can’t they stay in their own country? They are always telling us it is the Paradise of women.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: It is, Lady Caroline. That is why, like Eve, they are so extremely anxious to get out of it.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Who are Miss Worsley’s parents?
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: American women are wonderfully clever in concealing their parents.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: My dear Lord Illingworth, what do you mean? Miss Worsley, Caroline, is an orphan. Her father was a very wealthy millionaire or philanthropist, or both, I believe, who entertained my son quite hospitably, when he visited Boston. I don’t know how he made his money, originally.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I fancy in American dry goods.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: What are American dry goods?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: American novels.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: How very singular! . . . Well, from whatever source her large fortune came, I have a great esteem for Miss Worsley. She dresses exceedingly well. All Americans do dress well. They get their clothes in Paris.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: They say, Lady Hunstanton, that when good Americans die they go to Paris.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Indeed? And when bad Americans die, where do they go to?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Oh, they go to America.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I am afraid you don’t appreciate America, Lord Illingworth. It is a very remarkable country, especially considering its youth.
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: The youth of America is their oldest tradition. It has been going on now for three hundred years. To hear them talk one would imagine they were in their first childhood. As far as civilisation goes they are in their second.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: There is undoubtedly a great deal of corruption in American politics. I suppose you allude to that?
units.name: KELVIL

units.text: I wonder.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH
